correctness.rationale: For a fixed k-set of roots, the complete directed rooted-forest determinant on the n−k nonroots is det(nI−J)=k n^{n−k−1} when k<n, and the empty minor is 1 when k=n. Independently choose a permutation on the k roots, allowing fixed points. Thus the claimed multiplicity is exact, with no empty cyclic set. Boolean characters diagonalize the symmetric counting convolution (no n^n normalization). The size-k signed sum is the kth coefficient of g(z)=(1−z)^s(1+z)^{n−s}; integrating z g′(z) at z=t/n with e^(−t) gives the required k·k! factor. Differentiation produces the bracket n−2s−t after substitution, strictly negative at t>0 even at the midpoint. The exponent s−1 is even for the claimed sector and can only add an isolated zero (or none), so the integral is strictly negative. At s=n the factor (1+t/n)^(−1) cancels because the bracket is −n−t. Summing multiplicities gives H_n; the ordinary upper binomial tail is 2^{n−1}+O(2^n/√n) and its alternating correction is exactly (−1)^m binom(n−1,m−1) for m=⌈n/2⌉. Taking half the difference proves the limit of H_n/2^n, not a limit for the actual inertia fraction. The qualifying sector is nonempty also for n=2, where s=1 lies at the midpoint. A fresh direct check grouped cyclic vertices as the image of f^n, enumerated all maps for n=2–5, and matched the exact multipliers (n=2 has weight-ordered multipliers 4,−2,0). Replay: the fixed-root minor, coefficient formula and derivative can all be reconstructed in RESULT.md lines 20–45; finite checks do not establish all-order signs for any other sector.

value.rationale: The cyclic-vertex set is a basic random mapping statistic. Pairwise information or nonvanishing does not resolve the real signature of its convolution. The result gives strict negativity in a uniform sector of every dimension and at least quarter asymptotic density in the guaranteed sector, not merely a failure of positive semidefiniteness in small examples. This is an independently useful partial spectral classification even without a full inertia or invertibility theorem.
